B In addition, all pregnant women 24 years and younger and other pregnant women at increased risk should be screened. B

background.definition: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra which commonly presents as dysuria or urethral discharge. Chronic urethritis, also called urethral syndrome, is an ill-defined symptom complex believed to be due to dysfunctional urinary epithelium, including patients with interstitial cystitis.

list.listitem: Although the precise incidence is unknown, there has been increased reporting of urethritis concomitant with a resurgence of STIs in the Western world.

The annual incidence of STIs in the United States (US) is increasing and it is estimated to be 26.2 million cases among persons aged 15 to 39 years (2018), including 4 million reported incident cases of chlamydia and 1.6 million incident cases of gonorrhea.
From 2018 to 2022, the incidence of chlamydia decreased by 10% and gonorrhea increased by 5% in women in the United States based on CDC surveillance reporting.
One in 4 adolescent girls between the ages of 14 and 19 years is estimated to have at least one of the most common STIs (human papillomavirus, chlamydia, herpes simplex virus, and trichomoniasis).

Women who have sex exclusively with women have lower rates of STIs than women who have sex with men. Trichomonas is more common than chlamydia and gonorrhea in women who exclusively have sex with women.
In one screening study of adolescent girls seen in family planning, STI, or school-based clinics, 29% had at least 1 positive test for chlamydia.

The annual prevalence of STIs in the US is estimated to be 67.6 million cases among persons aged 15 to 39 years (2018), including 2.4 million prevalent cases of chlamydia and 209,000 overall prevalent cases of gonorrhea.
Worldwide, the prevalence of gonorrhea in pregnant women was estimated at 1.85%, with the highest rate in the African region (3.53%) and the lowest rate in the European region (0.52%).
Individuals infected with STIs shoulder a tremendous physical, social, psychological, and economic burden, incurring an estimated cost of up to $14.7 billion annually.

The most recent figures (2018) estimate $15.9 billion (25th–75th percentile: $14.9–16.9 billion) in discounted, lifetime direct medical costs; most due to sexually-acquired HIV ($13.7 billion) and HPV ($0.8 billion).

Estimated lifetime medical costs per infection for men and women, respectively, based on 2018 data, were $46 (95% credibility interval, $32-$62) and $262 ($127-$483) for chlamydia, $78 ($36-$145) and $254 ($96-$518) for gonorrhea, and $5 ($1-$14) and $36 ($17-$58) for trichomoniasis.
The etiology can be infectious (bacterial, viral, protozoal) or noninfectious (ie, traumatic, chemical, inflammatory, tumor, atrophy) (see ).

Most commonly a presentation of a nonulcerative genital STI. Chlamydia trachomatis
C and Neisseria gonorrhea (GC) are the most commonly reported STIs associated with urethritis in women. Chlamydia, trichomoniasis, genital herpes, and human papillomavirus (HPV) comprise 97.6% of all prevalent and 93.1% of all incident STIs, based on 2018 US population data. Other agents are listed in .

Based on surveillance data from sexual health clinics in 6 cities, Mycoplasma genitalium was identified in 26.8% of cases with urethritis overall, but less commonly in females. Macrolide resistance was high.
Urethritis is also associated with other infectious genitourinary conditions including cervicitis, urinary tract infection (UTI), pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and pyelonephritis.
Chronic urethritis in children and urethritis associated with interstitial cystitis is believed to be caused by dysfunctional urinary epithelium.
Instrumentation (eg, catheterization) and physical trauma (eg, childbirth) are also associated with urethritis.

Urethritis is primarily due to infectious agents ascending from the periurethral skin and distal urethra. Hematogenous spread can also occur. Whether infection occurs is based on multiple factors including pathogenicity of the agent, inoculum size, and host defenses (including genetic factors).

Similarly, antibiotic susceptibility to gonococcal infection is associated with host factors such as mutations in the efflux pump mtrCDE operon and farAB; mutations that are overrepresented in cervical relative to urethral isolates.

A molecular model posed to explain why women with gonococcal infection are often asymptomatic notes that gonococcal engagement of complement receptor 3 (alternate complement pathway) on the cervical epithelia causes ruffling that does not promote inflammation.
Idiopathic urethritis in children may be due to dysfunctional elimination.
Asymptomatic urethritis is sometimes associated with STIs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Younger age (15-24 years; chlamydia 65% and gonorrhea 1/2 of all reported cases)
Oral contraceptive or intrauterine device use (chlamydia)

list.listitem: The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening for chlamydia in all sexually-active nonpregnant women 24 years and younger and older women who are at increased risk. A In addition, all pregnant women 24 years and younger and other pregnant women at increased risk should be screened. B
Patient education can reduce the risk of STI. B
The USPSTF (2020) recommends intensive behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. B
Because chlamydia is the most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU), screening for chlamydia in high-risk populations is important for prevention.

The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening for chlamydia in all sexually active nonpregnant women 24 years and younger and older women who are at increased risk. In addition, all pregnant women 24 years and younger and older pregnant women at increased risk should be screened.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevenction (2021) recommend that all sexually-active transgender men and nonbinary persons aged <25 years with a cervix should be screened for gonorrhea and chlamydia on an annual basis. Additional recommendations are provided for gender diverse persons.
An intensive patient education intervention (three 3- to 4-hour sessions) was found to reduce the likelihood of at least 1 gonorrhea or chlamydia infection (16.8% vs 26.9%; NNT = 12).

The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence concluded that the balance of evidence marginally supports one-to-one counseling intervention for the prevention of STIs. Interventions including multiple sessions may be most effective.
There is good evidence that nonoxynol-9 does not protect against STI and may increase the rate of genital ulceration.

A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in the United Kingdom did not show that test messaging, specifically to improve sex behaviors, reduced the incidence of chlamydia and gonorrhea reinfection at one year in people aged 16-24 years.

Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (Doxy PEP), while showing effectiveness in cisgender men and transgender women, was not shown to be effective in cisgender women in reducing rates of chlymiyai, gonorrhea, nr syphilis in a randomized trial in Kenya, although use of doxycycline in the treatment group was low.

STI Treatment Guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (2021) recommend that for the diagnosis of urethritis, patients should have symptoms (eg, discharge, dysuria), physical signs (urethral discharge), or positive laboratory testing (eg, Gram stain, culture, or PCR). A Gram stain of urethral secretions is considered positive if 5 or more WBCs per oil immersion field are identified. C
Test for chlamydia with an NAAT. B
Test for gonorrhea by culture, NAAT, or nucleic acid hybridization test. NAATs are more sensitive than culture, which is helpful if drug resistance gonorrhea is suspected. B
Rapid point-of-care rapid testing of vaginal swabs can also be used for detection of chlamydia and gonorrhea in women. (SORT C)

May have dysuria, vaginal discharge (curd-like, fishy odor), positive wet prep, and negative urine culture
May have dysuria, postcoital bleeding, dyspareunia, and older age group
Frequency with small-volume voiding, urgency, dysuria, and pain without evidence of UTI
Mucopurulent discharge from the cervix, and dysuria not prominent feature
Pelvic pain, discharge from cervical os, and constitutional symptoms
Acute onset dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pressure/pain, fever, nausea, flank pain and positive urine culture

list.listitem: Patients often present with focal genitourinary symptoms including dysuria, urgency, frequency, vaginal discharge (mucopurulent), or abnormal vaginal bleeding; some women are asymptomatic, and most women with chlamydia infection are asymptomatic.
Symptoms may develop insidiously or occur acutely.
Fever may indicate cystitis, pyelonephritis, PID, or systemic gonorrhea; proctitis (purulent anal discharge, anal pruritus, tenesmus or rectal bleeding) or pharyngitis can also occur with gonorrhea.
Intermittent dysuria, simulating UTI, is common with chlamydia urethritis.
Oculogenital syndrome (conjunctivitis accompanied by urethritis) has been documented secondary to chlamydia infection.

Reiter's syndrome (a group of inflammatory conditions involving joints, urethra, eyes, and skin mucous membranes) is commonly associated with chlamydia; symptoms typically present 1 to 3 weeks after acute infection.
Ask about vaginal discharge (vaginitis, cervicitis), pelvic pain (PID), and pruritus (vaginitis, perianal conditions).

Patient demographics (eg, ethnicity, inner city population, and patient under age 25 years), previous history of symptoms, and personal history of drug or alcohol abuse, sexual assault, or incarceration should be noted.

If urethral discharge is present, ask about duration, nature, quantity, and quality (mucoid, serous, or purulent). Ask about any history of recent trauma from various causes, such as bicycling, menstrual history (age of onset, regularity, intermenstrual bleeding [cervicitis/cervical lesions], and postcoital bleeding [atrophic vaginitis, cervicitis, tumor]).

A sexual history should include 6-month risk assessment (number of partners, frequency of sexual activity, partner gender and their symptom status, orogenital sex, using sex toys, and sex with persons who use illicit substances).

Past medical history should include previous STIs, PID, vaginitis, cervicitis, UTIs, vaginismus, dyspareunia (PID, atrophic vaginitis), and infertility (PID). Surgical history should include any urogenital surgeries and urologic procedures.

Examine the lower abdomen, perineum, genitalia, and rectum, looking for signs of atrophic changes, discharge, ulcers, warts, or other lesions. Examine the urethra for signs of inflammation of the meatus, edema, or tenderness. Structural abnormalities such as urethral caruncle, urethral diverticulum, cystocele, urethrocele, rectocele, uterine, or mucosal prolapse may be detected.

Urethral discharge may be present, but the physical characteristics of the discharge do not help confirm the etiology. To elicit discharge, gently compress and "strip" the urethra between the symphysis pubis and the anterior vaginal wall with the gloved finger from intravaginally outward. Send any material obtained for Gram stain.

Assess vaginal discharge, obtained from the posterior vaginal wall, for color, consistency, odor, and pH measurement; consider a saline and potassium hydroxide preparation (wet prep) to diagnose vaginitis.

On speculum examination, note cervical characteristics including appearance, shape, edema, friability (easy bleeding on touch), lesions, and discharge. Obtain vaginal discharge from the posterior vaginal wall for testing. Obtain a cervical specimen for testing when appropriate.
The pelvic examination, if needed, should include evaluation of the uterus, tubes, ovaries, bladder, and adnexa for pain or masses.

Appropriate specimens for confirmation of chlamydia or gonorrhea can be obtained by insertion of a small intraurethral or intracervical swab. Self-swabbing for chlamydia and gonorrhea has high sensitivity and specificity (91% and 99%, respectively; LR+91, LR− 0.09). The specimen can be sent for PCR testing or culture or for urine PCR or NAAT.
Test for chlamydia using NAAT. C
Test for gonorrhea by culture, NAAT, or nucleic acid hybridization test. NAATs are more sensitive than culture. C
Screening for gonorrhea and chlamydia can be performed using a NAAT on urine. This may be the most cost-effective screening method if a pelvic examination is not otherwise needed.

Authors of a 2023 meta-analysis found vaginal swabs provided better sensitivity over urine sampling for women being tested for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and/or trichomoniasis. Pooled sensitivity estimates for vaginal swabs and urine, respectively, were 94.1% and 86.9% for chlamydia, 96.5% and 90.7% for gonorrhea, and 98.0% and 95.1% for trichomoniasis, with all P values <.001.
Automated urine flow cytometry of first void urine improves specificity over microscopy for predicting C. trachomatis or M. genitalium infection.

Culture is available for detection of rectal, oropharyngeal, and conjunctival gonococcal infection, as NAAT is not FDA-cleared for use with these specimens. CDC recommends performing culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in cases of suspected or documented treatment failure, because non-culture tests can’t provide antimicrobial susceptibility results.

Rapid point-of-care (POC) testing of vaginal swabs was approved by the FDA in 2021 for chlamydia and gonorrhea testing in women. The test is CLIA waived and takes 30 minutes to obtain results. The overall sensitivity and specificity of the Binx IO POC test for chlamydia was 96.1% and 99.1%, respectively. The overall sensitivity and specificity for gonorrhea was 100% and 99.9%, respectively.

In a study comparing clinical performance of four multiplex real-time PCR commercial kits for the detection of sexually-transmitted pathogens - STI PLUS ELITe MGB kit (ELITechGroup), N. gonorrhoeae/C. trachomatis/M. genitalium/T.vaginalis Real-TM kit (Sacace Biotechnologies), Allplex STI Essential kit (Seegene), and FTD Urethritis Plus kit (Fast-Track Diagnostics), all showed good performances for detection of C. trachomatis, but the Seegene and Sacace kits showed low positive agreement for the detection of N. gonorrhoeae.
Use of microscopy in the diagnosis of NGU was found to be inconsistent between microscopists with poor sensitivity.
First-void urine showing positive leukocyte esterase or >/=10 WBCs/hpf under microscopy on spun urine can be indicative of urethritis.
Patients often present with dysuria, urgency, frequency, vaginal discharge (mucopurulent), or abnormal vaginal bleeding; some are asymptomatic.
Transgender and non-binary individuals with urethritis symptoms should be offered testing and treatment that is consistent with their sexual anatomy and sexual practices.

STI Treatment Guidelines from the CDC (2021) recommend that for the diagnosis of urethritis, patients should have symptoms (eg, discharge, dysuria), physical signs (urethral discharge), or positive laboratory testing (eg, urine leukocytes, microscopic pyuria, Gram stain, culture, and PCR). A Gram stain of urethral secretions is considered positive if 5 or more WBCs per oil immersion field are identified.

Self-taken vaginal swabs by women who suspect they have a STI, with subsequent nucleic acid amplification testing (Gen-Probe), are more sensitive than clinician-obtained swabs for identifying women with either gonorrhea or chlamydia infection. A patient-administered vaginal PCR swab in one study had a LR+ of 99 and an LR- of 0.09.
See .

Treat women with urethritis suspected of having a sexually transmitted infection (STI) for both gonorrhea and chlamydia with single-dose IM ceftriaxone 500 mg plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. If pregnant, use ceftriaxone plus a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally. Patients weighing more than 300 pounds should be given 1 gram of ceftriaxone. A

When urethral discharge is recurrent or persistent, treat with single-dose metronidazole (2 g orally) OR single-dose tinidazole (2 g orally) AND single-dose azithromycin (1 g orally) if not used for the initial episode. A
Drug treatment, based on diagnosis, is shown in .
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines (2021) recommend treating for suspected STIs with antibiotics, as soon as urethritis is diagnosed.

The recommended regimen for women with urethritis suspected of having a STI, to cover for both gonorrhea and chlamydia, is single-dose IM ceftriaxone 500 mg plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. If pregnant, use ceftriaxone plus a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally. Patients weighing more than 300 pounds should be given 1 gram of ceftriaxone.

Among women with urogenital chlamydia, authors of a Cochrane review were unable to determine whether azithromycin compared to doxycycline increased the risk of microbiological failure, although azithromycin probably slightly reduces adverse events.

A 2022 RCT in France showed a higher cure rate for anorectal chlamydial infection with doxycycline (94% cure rate using 100 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to azithromycin (85% cure rate using 1000 mg once daily) in women with concurrent vaginal chlamydia.
If urethral irritation is believed to be due to menopause, consider hormone therapy or lubricants.
If you suspect that chronic urethritis is associated with interstitial cystitis, see treatment recommendations in that chapter.
Local anesthetics, antispasmodics, muscle relaxants, tricyclic antidepressants and alpha blockers may be tried as supportive therapy.
Patients with urethral caruncle-associated symptoms are usually treated with simple excision of the lesion, but data are extremely limited.

Information on optimal handling of partner notification/treatment is limited. Authors of a Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence that expedited partner therapy was better than patient referral for preventing re-infection of index patients and number of partners treated. Many studies, however, suffered from high attrition. Expedited partner therapy was not superior to enhanced patient referral in preventing re-infection in three trials. Partner home sampling kits did not result in lower rates of re-infection of index cases.

Treat partners (within the preceding 60 days) of women with STIs or refer them for treatment. Familiarize yourself with state regulations and CDC advice governing whether or not partners may be treated without direct examination.

One study found that treating partners immediately (through medication given directly to patients or offering medications to partners without seeing them) resulted in fewer gonococcal infections (but not chlamydial infections) at follow-up (3% vs 11%; NNT = 12.5).

Retreat patients with antibiotics only when there is objective evidence of recurrence of urethritis. If the patient did not comply with initial treatment or was re-exposed by the same inadequately treated partner, then give a full course of appropriate therapy to both.

Hospitalization may be required with severe PID or tubo-ovarian abscess, suspected ectopic pregnancy, disseminated gonococcal disease (suspect with fever, skin lesions, arthralgias, and tenosynovitis), or severe inflammatory disorders such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or severe Reiter's syndrome.
Urethral stricture may be a consequence of urethritis, especially gonococcal urethritis. When stricture is present, urology referral is warranted.
Infertility or subsequent ectopic pregnancy can also be late complications of STIs.

Most patients do well with initial treatment for dual infections (chlamydia and gonorrhea). Teenagers may be more prone to recurrence due to lack of adherence to treatment and high rates of reinfection. C

Most patients do well with initial treatment for dual infections (chlamydia and gonorrhea). Teenagers may be more prone to recurrence due to lack of adherence to treatment and high rates of reinfection.

In a study of individuals diagnosed with uncomplicated gonorrhea or chlamydia infection recruited from 3 sexual health clinics in England, the median time to clearance of infection was 4 days (IQR 2-10 days) for gonococcal infection and 10 days (IQR 7-14 days) for chlamydia infection.
Symptoms of Reiter's syndrome may persist.
Prompt treatment of PID may reduce complications (eg, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain).
Women diagnosed with a new STI should be recommended for testing for other STIs including syphilis, and human immunodeficiency virus.

Test of cure for chlamydia and gonococcal urethritis following completion of recommended therapy is recommended for pregnant women (3-4 weeks after treatment) or if symptoms persist. Because reinfection rates are high, nonpregnant women and men should be considered for re-screening at 3 months after initial infection.
Consider culture and antibiotic susceptibility testing in any patient with suspected gonorrhea treatment failure.
Many cases of urethritis are related to STI.
Sexual education and safe sex (eg, use of condoms, single partner) can help reduce infection rates.
Sexual partners (preceding 60 days) need to be treated.
If symptoms persist, follow-up testing and treatment are needed; sexual abstinence during the treatment period (or for 7 days with single-dose therapy) is needed to prevent spread.

Older women are less likely to have an underlying STI, although a thorough sexual history should be taken. A negative screen for STI should prompt evaluation for other causes including hormone deficiency, chemical irritation, cystitis, and tumor.

Certain drugs, including quinolones and tetracycline, are contraindicated in pregnancy. For chlamydia in pregnancy, options include azithromycin (1 g orally in single dose, recommended by CDC) or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days. Erythromycin estolate is contraindicated in pregnancy but erythromycin base may be used.

In one study, children with idiopathic urethritis randomized to bowel and bladder regimens, biofeedback, and/or alpha-blockers when sphincter dyssynergia was identified had a higher full response to treatment than those randomized to treatment with antibiotics, analgesics, and/or anticholinergic agents (83% vs 35%; NNT = 2).

cell.label: Patient presents with dysuria. History and/or physical examination positive for urethral or cervical mucopurulent discharge?
Perimenopausal or menopausal woman with other genitourinary symptoms (eg, dyspareunia and vaginal dryness)?
Suspect menopause-related; consider hormone or lubricant treatment.
Additional symptoms of UTI (eg, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain)?
Suspect UTI. Treat or test (eg, urinalysis) and treat. If symptoms persist, test for STI.
Obtain specimen(s) (ie, intrameatal, intravaginal/intracervical, and urine). Run PCR, NAAT, or send for culture.
Pelvic pain, uterine tenderness, constitutional symptoms?
Vaginal symptoms predominate (eg, itching and odor).
Suspect vaginitis; test (eg, wet prep) and treat.

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: NAAT, nucleic acid amplification test; PCR, polymerase chain reaction; PID, pelvic inflammatory disease; STI, sexually transmitted infection.
